readings.c1s2:
as, an ''uneventful'' reign or life. ''Southey.''

¶
'''uneventfully''' (un-ē̤-vent′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In an uneventful manner; so as to be without striking occurrences.

'''unevident''' (un-ev′i-dent), ''a.'' Not evident, clear, obvious, or manifest; obscure. ''Bp. Hacket,'' Abp. Williams, i. 197. (''Davies.'')

'''unexact''' (un-eg-zakt′), ''a.'' Inexact. ''Imp. Dict.'' [Rare.]

'''unexaminable''' (un-eg-zam′i-na-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being or proper to be examined.
{{smaller block|The lowly, alwise, and ''unexaminable'' intention of Christ in what he went with resolution to doe.
{{right|''Milton,'' Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}

'''unexampled''' (un-eg-zam′pld), ''a.'' Having no example or similar case; having no precedent or rival; unprecedented; unparalleled. ''Milton,'' P. L., iii. 410.
{{smaller block|<poem>Her modest mien
And carriage, marked by ''unexampled'' grace.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth,'' Prelude, vii.}}}}

'''unexceptionable''' (un-ek-sep′shọn-a-bl), ''a.'' Not liable to any exception or objection; unobjectionable; faultless; hence, excellent; admirable.
{{smaller block|Men of clear and ''unexceptionable'' characters.
{{right|''Waterland,'' Works, V. 296.}}}}

'''unexceptionableness''' (un-ek-sep′shọn-a-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unexceptionable. ''Dr. H. More,'' Seven Churches, Pref.

'''unexceptionably''' (un-ek-sep′shọn-a-bli), ''adv.'' In an unexceptionable manner. ''South,'' Ser-
readings.c1s3:
mons, V. iv.

'''unexceptional''' (un-ek-sep′shon-al), ''a.'' Not forming an exception; in the regular course; usual.

'''unexceptionally''' (un-ek-sep′shon-al-i), ''adv.'' Without exception; in a manner excluding nothing; entirely.

'''unexceptive''' (un-ek-sep′tiv), ''a.'' Not exceptive; admitting no exception. ''J. H. Sterling'', Text-book to Kant, p. 11.

'''unexcised''' (un-ek-sīzd′), ''a.'' Not charged with the duty of excise; not subject to the payment of excise.

'''unexclusive''' (un-eks-klö′siv), ''a.'' Not exclusive; general; comprehensive.
{{smaller block|His erudition was as ''unexclusive'' as profound.
{{right|''Sir W. Hamilton.''}}}}

'''unexclusively''' (un-eks-klö′siv-li), ''adv.'' Without exclusion of anything; so as not to exclude. ''Sir W. Hamilton'', Reid’s Works, Supp. Diss., Note D, § 2.

'''unexcogitable''' (un-eks-koj′i-ta-bl), ''a.'' Not excogitable; inconceivable. ''Sir W. Raleigh'', Hist. World, I. 2.

'''unexcusable''' (un-eks-kū′za-bl), ''a.'' Inexcusable. ''Fuller'', General Worthies.

'''unexcusableness''' (un-eks-kū′za-bl-nes), ''n.'' Inexcusableness. ''Hammond'', Works, IV. 642.
readings.c2s1:
inactive.

{{smaller block|<poem>You therein
. . . leave ''unexecuted'' your own renowned knowledge.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 7. 45.}}}}

¶
'''unexempt''' (un-eg-zemt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not exempt; not free by privilege.—'''2†.''' Not exempting from or depriving of some privilege or the like. ''Milton'', Comus, l. 685.

'''unexpectant''' (un-eks-pek′tant), ''a.'' Not expectant; not expecting, looking for, or eagerly waiting for something.

{{smaller block|With bent ''unexpectant'' faces. ''George Eliot'', Romola, lv.}}

'''unexpectation†''' (un-eks-pek-tā′shọn), ''n.'' Want of previous consideration; want of foresight. ''Bp. Hall'', Balm of Gilead, § 1.

'''unexpected''' (un-eks-pek′ted), ''a.'' Not expected; not looked for; unforeseen; sudden: often used substantively with the definite article: as, it is ''the unexpected'' that happens.

{{smaller block|<poem>Thy speech doth please me; for it ever sounds
As thou brought’st joyful, ''unexpected'' news.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iv. 4.}}}}

'''unexpectedly''' (un-eks-pek′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an unexpected manner; at a time or in a manner not expected or looked for; suddenly. ''Milton'', S. A., l. 1750.

'''unexpectedness''' (un-eks-pek′ted-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unexpected. ''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, iv. 29.

'''unexpedient''' (un-eks-pē′di-ent), ''a.'' Inexpedient. ''Milton'', Education. [Rare.]

'''unexpensive''' (un-eks-pen′siv), ''a.'' Inexpensive. ''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''unexperience†''' (un-eks-pē′ri-ens), ''n.'' Inexperience. ''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iii. 4.

'''unexperienced''' (un-eks-pē′ri-ẹnst), ''a.'' '''1.''' Inexperienced.
{{smaller block|Thou return ''unexperienced'' to thy grave.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 1. 86.}}
Young at his first entrance, and ''unexperienc’d'', he [Ethelbert] was the first raiser of civill War among the Saxons.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., iii.}}}}
'''2.''' Untried; not yet known from experience; also, exhibiting inexperience: applied to things.
{{smaller block|''Unexperienced'' art.
{{right|''G. Harvey'', Four Letters.}}}}

'''unexperient†''' (un-eks-pē′ri-ẹnt), ''a.'' Inexperienced. ''Shak.'', Lover’s Complaint, l. 318.

'''unexpert''' (un-eks-pėrt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Inexpert. ''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 1.
{{smaller block|<poem>My sentence is for open war; of wiles
More ''unexpert'' I boast not; them let those
Contrive who need, or when they need.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 52.}}}}
'''2.''' Without knowledge; unacquainted; ignorant.
{{smaller block|<poem>Him you will find in letters and in laws
Not ''unexpert''.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Imit. of Horace, i. 9.}}}}

'''unexpertly''' (un-eks-pėrt′li), ''adv.'' Inexpertly.

'''unexplored''' (un-eks-plōrd′), ''a.'' Not explored, in any sense.

'''unexposed''' (un-eks-pōzd′), ''a.'' Not exposed, in any sense.

'''unexpressible''' (un-eks-pres′i-bl), ''a.'' Inexpressible. ''Milton'', Church-Government, ii. 2.

'''unexpressibly''' (un-eks-pres′i-bli), ''adv.'' Inexpressibly. ''Bp. Hall'', Character of Man.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''unexpressive''' (un-eks-pres′iv), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not expressive; deficient in expression.—'''2†.''' Not to be expressed; inexpressible; unutterable; ineffable. ''Shak.'', As you Like it, iii. 2. 10.

'''unextended''' (un-eks-ten′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not extended or stretched out.
{{smaller block|''Unextended'' arms. {{right|''Congreve'', Mourning Bride, iii.}}}}
'''2.''' Not having extension; occupying no assignable space.
{{smaller block|A spiritual, that is, an ''unextended'' substance.
{{right|''Locke'', Human Understanding, iv. 10.}}}}

'''unextinguishable''' (un-eks-ting′gwish-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Inextinguishable.
{{smaller block|''Unextinguishable'' fire. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 88.}}}}

'''unextinguishably''' (un-eks-ting′gwish-a̤-bli), ''adv.'' Inextinguishably.

'''unextricable''' (un-eks′tri-ka-bl), ''a.'' Inextricable. ''Barrow'', Sermons, III. xxxvi.

'''uneyed†''' (un-īd′), ''a.'' Unobserved; unnoticed; unseen; unperceived. ''Beau. and Fl.'', Wit at Several Weapons, ii.

'''unfabled''' (un-fā′bld), ''a.'' Not fabled or imaginary; not mentioned in fable; unconnected or unmixed with fable; real.
{{smaller block|They are more amusing than plain ''unfabled'' precept.
{{right|''Sydney Smith'', Works, I. 176. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unface''' (un-fās′), ''v. t.'' To remove the face or cover from; expose.
readings.c3s1:
ing, perishing, or withering.
{{smaller block|A crown incorruptible, ''unfadable.''
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, Ahasuerus Feasting.}}}}

¶
'''unfadging†''' (un-faj′ing), ''a.'' Not suiting; of unsuitable shape, quality, or the like.
{{smaller block|The potter may err in framing his vessel, and so in anger dash the ''unfadging'' clay against the walls.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Sermons, III. 122. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unfading''' (un-fā′ding), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not liable to lose strength or freshness of coloring.—'''2.''' Not liable to wither or decay.
{{smaller block|The ''unfading'' rose of Eden. ''Pope'', Eloisa to Abelard.}}

'''unfadingly''' (un-fā′ding-li), ''adv.'' In an unfading manner; so as not to fade; imperishably.

'''unfadingness''' (un-fā′ding-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unfading. ''Polwhele'', Hist. Devonshire.

'''unfailable†''' (un-fā′la̤-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of failing; infallible.
{{smaller block|This ''unfailable'' word of truth.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Sermon on 2 Pet. i. 10.}}}}

'''unfailableness†''' (un-fā′la-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unfailable; infallibility.

'''unfailing''' (un-fā′ling), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not liable to fail; incapable of being exhausted: as, an ''unfailing'' spring; ''unfailing'' sources of supply.—'''2.''' Not missing; always fulfilling a hope, promise, or want; not coming short; sure; certain.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou, secure of my ''unfailing'' word.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Iliad, i. 322.}}
<poem>Some god, propitious to the Trojan foe,
Has from my arm ''unfailing'' struck the bow.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xv. 551.}}}}
